utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, everybody, and good morning to you, Madam Registrar. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-05-88-T, The Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic, et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, ma'am. All the accused are present. Prosecution, it's Mr. McCloskey and Mr. Vanderpuye who are present today. Amongst the Defence teams, I notice the absence of Mr. Nikolic from the Beara team, Mr. Bourgon from the Nikolic team, Mr. Petrusic from the Miletic team, and that's it. Today we are going to start -- do you have any preliminaries by the way? I am informed that we are to expect some filings from the Prosecution in response to some of the Borovcanin motions; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm told we filed some motions on Friday, three.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Your Honour, one preliminary in relation to that. We plan to be filing a reply in response to the motion in respect of protective measures. So we would kindly request that the Chamber hold off for a couple of days so that we have an opportunity to make that application.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Thank you. So today we start with the Borovcanin Defence. Is there going to be an opening statement? Yes, Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. There will be an opening statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How long do you intend to be speaking?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I hope not to exceed 45 minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours. I am privileged to appear before you this morning to present the opening statement on behalf of Mr. Ljubomir Borovcanin. Your Honours, at the risk of oversimplifying a very complicated and extensive indictment, Mr. Borovcanin is essentially charged with two overarching crimes: Forcibly transferring the civilian population of Srebrenica and mass murdering the military aged men of Srebrenica. The Prosecution says that is he committed these crimes as part of a joint criminal enterprise to which he contributed by allowing men under his command to assist with the evacuation of Potocari on the 12th and 13th of July, knowing that the civilians had been, and were being, coerced to leave. As to the mass murder and genocide charge, the Prosecution alleges that Mr. Borovcanin allowed his units to assist in the separation of military aged men at Potocari, knowing that they were going to be killed. They also alleged that he assisted and ordered his units to take prisoners along the Konjevic Polje road on the 13th of July, again knowing that they would all be killed, not only knowing that they would all be killed, but intending that they would all be killed. Your Honours, the case against Mr. Borovcanin is based upon the fallacy of omniscience. The Prosecution imputes to Mr. Borovcanin knowledge of everything that happened in Srebrenica before his arrival there on the 11th of July, and they impute to him knowledge of everything that would happen after the 12th and 13th of July. Now, the Prosecution is, of course, perfectly entitled to build case on inference, to invite you to draw inferences as to his state of mind and his state of knowledge based upon his conduct. But to establish that he knew and intended that these mass killings would occur, and that he was participating in them, they must show you that that is the only reasonable conclusion consistent with his actions. In our view, the evidence presented by the Prosecution does not show that. On the contrary, the evidence shows that Mr. Borovcanin did his best to act lawfully and honourably despite the difficult circumstances that he was facing and that were not of his creation. We have nevertheless decided, even though we believe that already the evidence is not sufficient, to offer additional evidence on limited topics, hoping that it will assist you to understand Mr. Borovcanin's position at the time and the circumstances that he was facing. Our evidence will focus on five issues: First, the nature of Mr. Borovcanin's authority as a MUP commander assigned to a VRS zone of responsibility; second, the ad hoc and transitory nature of his command to the units that he had not previously commanded without the assistance of any command staff or even a deputy commander; third, the character of the units assigned to him, which included a group of ill-trained deserters; fourth, the limited scope of his involvement in relation to prisoners of war; and, fifth, the nature of the military threat facing his units on the ground and the reasonableness of detaining large numbers of military aged men in civilian clothing from the enclave. What I propose to do in this opening statement, Your Honours, is to summarize the Prosecution case, and to highlight for you the specific areas on which we will be presenting evidence. We believe that this summary is indispensable to understanding the relevance of the information that you'll be hearing, particularly because there are many aspects of the Prosecution case that we do not dispute. Our point of disagreement with the Prosecution is their characterization of what Mr. Borovcanin knew and what reasonable inferences you, as a Trial Chamber, can draw from the circumstances about what he must have known. Let me start with the forcible transfer charge. You'll recall, Your Honours, that the Prosecution alleges that the criminal effort to forcibly transfer the civilian population of Srebrenica starts in March 1995. According to the Prosecution, supplies are progressively cut off to the enclave with the intention of forcing the civilians to leave. That effort then, according to the Prosecution, escalates on the 6th of July or about the 6th of July, when an armed defensive was commenced at least in part, according to the Prosecution, to terrorize the civilian population into leaving. This effort culminates in the takeover of Srebrenica town on the 11th of July. Now, Your Honours, what was Mr. Borovcanin doing throughout this period from March 1995 through the 11th of July 1995? How was he contributing to this alleged joint criminal enterprise? In fact, throughout that period, Mr. Borovcanin was 200 kilometres away engaged in intense combat with Bosnian armed forces in the area around Sarajevo. He was the deputy commander at the time and through July 1995 of the Special Police Brigade. As you'll hear from our first witness, Dr. Bajagic, the special police was a component of the Ministry Of The Interior akin to the gendarme or the carabinieri. Their purpose in peacetime was to respond to extreme civil unrest such as riots. During the war, however, they could be, and often were, deployed in combat. While in combat, they ceased to have any civil policing function and were subject to military command and military rules. From March 1995 until the 10th of July, Mr. Borovcanin was in the area of Sarajevo. To be precise, at Majevica and Treskavica. He had no involvement in the affairs of Srebrenica during that time. He received no orders, he received no planning documents, he received no reports. And, in fairness, the Prosecution hasn't suggested otherwise. On the 10th of July, he received an order from the MUP staff commander that he should go to Srebrenica to assist in combat tasks. The order indicated that the units -- the order indicated the units that would be under his command, and specifically directed him to report to General Krstic. This was in accordance with the usual procedure and applicable legislation. When acting in a combat role, MUP units were resubordinated to the VRS command in whose zone of responsibility they were to be deployed. Mr. Borovcanin followed this order, arriving in Bratunac on the 11th of July early in the afternoon. None of the units that were supposed to be assigned to him had yet arrived. He then went up to the Drina Corps forward command post at Pribicevac trying to obtain orders. He received some general instructions at that time from General Mladic over the telephone, and then returned to Bratunac. By then it was late afternoon, and the first of his three units that would eventually arrive had had arrived at that time. He sent them to the place where they would be billeted over night, and did not issue them any tasks or orders in relation to Potocari or Srebrenica. As it turned out, Mr. Borovcanin would not receive a concrete combat task until late on the evening of the 11th when he went and reconnoitered the terrain around Zuti Most. By this time, Your Honours, the Srebrenica enclave had already fallen. General Mladic, as you've seen on the trial video, had already strolled down the main street of Srebrenica town. The inhabitants of Srebrenica had already fled to Potocari, or they had assembled as part of the column and were preparing to break through towards Tuzla. You've seen the video of the chaos and the panic that already prevailed in the afternoon of the 11th of July. You have seen the displacement of the population to the factories in Potocari. All of this happens before Mr. Borovcanin has come near Potocari, much less issued any orders in support of any operation in relation to Srebrenica. Something else significant happens before Mr. Borovcanin has done anything in support of operations around Potocari. Colonel Karremans arrives at the Hotel Fontana on the evening of the 11th, and conveys a request to General Mladic that he says has come from the Bosnian government and from UNPROFOR that the refugees should be evacuated. You've seen that very request on the trial video. Now, why is this significant? It's significant, Your Honours, because it shows that the die has already been cast by the evening of the 11th of July. Whatever has happened to induce the refugees to leave Srebrenica had already happened and without any involvement or assistance of Mr. Borovcanin. The evacuation of the refugees by that point is an inevitability supported even by UNPROFOR and the Bosnian government. Now, as I just mentioned, late on the evening of the 11th of July, Mr. Borovcanin finally receives an order about what he will be doing the next day. He is told to prepare to secure the northern approaches to Potocari. On the morning of the 12th of July, Mr. Borovcanin follows that order and goes to Zuti Most. The three units that were assigned to him have arrived or do arrive and deploy to that area. Two of the units are MUP units: The 2nd Sekovici Detachment of the Special Police Brigade and the 1st PJP Company of the Zvornik Public Security Centre. We've already mentioned the Special Police Brigade. PJP units, as Dr. Bajagic will explain, are comprised of local police officers from a particular area who can be formed into a combat unit and deployed in combat. The third unit assigned to Mr. Borovcanin, as you'll hear during our case, was not even a unit in the true sense of the term. It was just a group of deserters who at that moment happened to be undergoing training at the MUP training facility in Jahorina. They were deserters in the true sense of the term. All of them had been arrested in Serbia or Montenegro and returned by force to the Republika Srpska. They were poorly trained and poorly motivated. All told, these three units under Mr. Borovcanin's command consisted of 250 men approximately. Now, one of the matters in which you will hear testimony from our expert witnesses is the ad hoc nature of Mr. Borovcanin's command. These three units were cobbled together extemporaneously and had never previously cooperated in a joint operation. They are put under his command temporarily. He has no command staff to assist him, he has no security organ, he has no logistics. He doesn't even have military lawyers to advise him on the legality of the orders that is he receiving at this time. He has no choice but to rely on the VRS commander in whose area of responsibility he is assigned, for logistical support, security support, and perhaps, most importantly, for information. Mr. Borovcanin himself spends most of that morning on the 12th of July between Zuti Most and Potocari, while his units move through the terrain on either side of the road. You've already heard some evidence during the Prosecution case about that movement. For the most part, we do not contest that evidence. Their task is to ensure that no BiH army forces are in the area. Now, remember, at this stage, the whereabouts of the 28th Division of the BiH army is unknown to the Serb forces. You will hear during our case from three members of the 1st PJP Company who confirm that they arrived at Zuti Most, that there were no hostilities there with UNPROFOR forces, that they moved through the terrain to the west of the road, that a soldier from the Bratunac Brigade was seriously injured by a land mine, and that having found no sign of Muslim forces, they return to the main road between Bratunac and Potocari, and that after waiting there for some period of time, they returned to Bratunac before being redeployed north along the Bratunac-Konjevic Polje road. Neither the 1st PJP Company, nor the 2nd Sekovici Detachment, had any involvement in the evacuation or separation of men in Potocari. Mr. Borovcanin himself moved up the main road towards Potocari, and he arrived there late in the morning of the 12th of July. He sees there an enormous crowd of civilians who are unmistakably waiting, waiting to be taken away, waiting to be evacuated, in fact, desperate to be evacuated. That's precisely what has already been agreed to by UNPROFOR, the VRS, and the Bosnian government. At some point around this time, Mr. Borovcanin has what, I think, can be fairly characterized as a verbal altercation with General Mladic. I won't remind you of the epithet Mladic uses to describe the MUP, according to PW-160. In any event, Mladic orders Borovcanin to deploy his two combat worthy units along the Bratunac-Konjevic Polje road in case the column of the 28th Division should attempt to go in that direction. Mladic also orders Mr. Borovcanin to leave behind his deserters unit in Potocari, to assist with the evacuation that he says has been agreed to. Now, let's be clear how important Mr. Borovcanin's response is from the Prosecution's perspective. According to the Prosecution theory, Mr. Borovcanin allowed his men to be used in the evacuation, not only to ensure the deportation and forcible transfer, but also to assist with the separation of the military-aged men, and I quote from paragraph 43 of the indictment: "... with full knowledge that those men would be summarily executed." Now, the Prosecution did not present any evidence showing that Mr. Borovcanin had been informed of any such thing. He wasn't at the Hotel Fontana meetings; he wasn't having private meetings with Generals Mladic or Krstic or Blagojevic; and as you'll hear from our expert Dr. Ristivojevic, his units had no particular role or responsibility in respect of prisoners of war. What the Prosecution is really saying is that leaving behind the Jahorina deserters for the purpose of the separations itself shows you that he had the knowledge and the intent of what was going -- of these criminal acts that are alleged. It also serves the purpose of showing not only that the detentions and the executions were going to take place, but that the forcible transfer was taking place. In other words, by this single action, two JCEs are conveniently established. Now, if any of us had been a lawyer on Mr. Borovcanin's nonexistent staff on the morning of the 12th of July, and we were asked to give an opinion on the legality of an order to assist with that evacuation which so we were told had been agreed to by the Bosnian government, by UNPROFOR, what would we have been able to say? Would we have really been able to say, "No, Mr. Borovcanin, you must not participate in this action because civilians may have been over the last week, over the last month, over the last several months, intimidated or coerced or otherwise improperly induced to leave"? Could we really say to him, "No, you can't participate," notwithstanding the circumstances of thousands of civilians who are desperate to leave? How would our analysis been affected if we knew that, in 1993, hundreds of civilians had been evacuated under the aegis of UNPROFOR and UNHCR? Well, we'll leave the answer to those questions, Your Honours, for closing arguments, but the point is that Mr. Borovcanin had complied with the order. He directed the commander of the Jahorina deserters to remain behind to assist in the evacuation. Evidence presented during the Prosecution case shows that Momir Nikolic then took charge of directing the evacuation operation. He was effectively in command of that unit during those two days. Now, what did Mr. Borovcanin see at Potocari while he was there on the 12th and 13th of July? Was there anything in the manner of the detention or separation that would have suggested that all those men were going to be slaughtered? Well, let's consider what Mr. Borovcanin could have seen on the 12th and 13th of July in Potocari. He left Potocari on the 12th before the separations began. He didn't return until the 13th, when he came back with the journalist for about half an hour to deal with the issue of the stolen water truck. On the 13th of July, as you've seen from the videotape shot that day, Mr. Borovcanin would have seen the men of military age being detained in a house opposite the DutchBat compound. But there's absolutely nothing improper or inappropriate in detaining suspected combatants, even if they are wearing civilian clothes. International humanitarian law allows that. In fact, reasonable grounds existed to presume that, in July 1995, all the men of military age were at least potentially combatants. We will present some of the very large number, the surprisingly large number, of BiH army documents showing that, by July 1995, the Srebrenica enclave was, to a very large extent, an armed camp. The purpose of this evidence, Your Honours, is not to establish any tu quoque way Defence. The purpose of this evidence, rather, is to show that it would have been entirely normal and prudent to detain every military-aged person leaving Srebrenica at that time. We will tender documents showing that the BiH Army had at least 6.000 armed combatants in Srebrenica, with as many as 10.000 more unarmed or periodically armed; that these men were organised into units, with defined zones of responsibility and specialists tasks; that teenagers as young as 15 years old were being inducted into the military; and that combatants often wore civilian clothing. The need for uniforms was so extreme, and the number required was so enormous, that on the 4th of June, Ramiz Becirovic, the Chief of Staff of the 28th Division in Srebrenica, sent a request for 7.000 uniforms to the 2nd Corps of the BiH Army. In this context, Your Honours, the detention of all military-aged men, would not, and should not have set off alarm bells that they were all going to be killed. Apart from this, the Prosecution points to the conditions of detention and the wholesale confiscation of belongings to suggest that this should have been evident. Again, Mr. Borovcanin's opportunity to observe that was limited. You yourselves have already seen about as much as Mr. Borovcanin could have seen on the 13th of July during the half hour that he was there. You see men crowded into the so-called White House, their belongings dumped on the ground outside. The grainy video of those men crowded together is a chilling sight in light of what we now know happened to many of them; but, at the time, nothing in those conditions would have indicated that they were all going to be executed en masse. Now, you've heard other evidence about violent acts taking place in Potocari on the 12th and 13th of July, about identification cards being burned or confiscated. We dispute these events occurred in the manner described by the Prosecution. But even if you accept that they did occur, there is simply no evidence whatsoever showing that Mr. Borovcanin observed these alleged incidents. Now, would it be natural to expect that he would be informed about those incidents? Well, Your Honours, as I previously mentioned, Momir Nikolic was in effective command of the men that he had left behind. Mr. Borovcanin had no particular role in regulating the detention of prisoners of war, and that will be confirmed by Dr. Ristivojevic who will explain that his units, in light of their lack of support, would only have responsibility at the point of surrender of a POW. On the 12th and 13th of July, Mr. Borovcanin was primarily preoccupied with deploying his units along the Konjevic Polje Road. Why was he doing that? He was doing that because there was a huge column consisting of between 12 and 15.000 people, many of whom were members of the 28th Division, and amongst whom 6 or 7.000 were armed. They were heading north parallel to the road between Bratunac and Konjevic Polje. Throughout the night of the 12th to the 13th, the road was an active combat zone. You've already heard some evidence about that fighting. You will hear more about it from three members of the PJP unit assigned there, two of whom were seriously wounded on the morning of the 13th. Now, that day, on the 13th, members of the Bosnian column started to surrender. Some were detained at the Sandici meadow. As you recall, General Mladic arrives, telling the men that they will be exchanged and sent to Kladanj or Tuzla. Mr. Borovcanin leaves the meadow before Mladic finishes speaking and proceeds north up the road. The prisoners are then apparently escorted or bused south from the meadow to the Kravica warehouse. The Prosecution's theory is that Mr. Borovcanin organised the detention of those men with the intention that they should be killed. They also allege that they were, in fact, killed by Mr. Borovcanin's subordinates at the Kravica warehouse. The cornerstone of the Prosecution case is the fact that Mr. Borovcanin passed in front of the Kravica warehouse on the afternoon of the 13th and saw bodies there, as you've seen from the Petrovic videotape. Let's consider a few aspects of this evidence, in particular as it relates to the critical issue of Mr. Borovcanin's intent. First, let's remember that Mr. Borovcanin walked into an interview with the Office of the Prosecutor in 2002, initially without a lawyer, and freely admitted that. He placed himself on the scene and said what he had seen. This is not the admission of a person -- this is not the admission a person is likely to make if they had participated and intended those killings. Now, the Prosecutor dismisses this, saying that Mr. Borovcanin had no choice but to make that admission. You remember during their opening statement, they indicated, and I quote: "Of course, he had to. It was on film, and it was acknowledged." Your Honours, where did that videotape come from? Mr. Borovcanin gave them that videotape. Let me say that again. The videotape showing the bodies in front of the Kravica warehouse was provided by Mr. Borovcanin at a time when the OTP did not have it. In other words, the very cornerstone, the crux of the Prosecution case is based on something that Mr. Borovcanin admitted and then supplied clear evidence was true. Mr. Borovcanin further explained in his interview that he stopped at the driveway to the warehouse compound, which is some distance down the road from the shots that you have seen on the video; that he was told that there had been an attempt by prisoners to escape; and that the people who had done the killings at the warehouse were not from the police. He then got back into his car and drove to Bratunac where he understood one of his officers was wounded. The Prosecution asks you to infer from these acts that Mr. Borovcanin intended that those men should all be killed, and that he was part of a joint criminal enterprise to that end. Your Honours, the Prosecution position defies common sense for several reasons. First, there is Mr. Borovcanin's own conduct in his interviews with the Office of the Prosecutor. The open avowal of what he saw when he did not have to is hardly the conduct of a man who actually did intend those killings. Second, Mr. Borovcanin was accompanied throughout the 13th of July by a journalist with a video camera who was filming indiscriminately whatever he saw. The Prosecution dismisses this individual as a quasi-journalist. Well, the point is, Your Honours, this individual was from a respected television station and he had a video camera. If Mr. Borovcanin had the intent that there would be massacres of Muslim detainees when he drove from Potocari, where he was dealing with the tank, up to Bratunac-Konjevic Polje road, would he really have taken someone with a video camera; or would he, rather, have simply dropped that person off in Bratunac on his way to the area? The Prosecution also alleges that Mr. Borovcanin had a duty to intervene based on what he saw at that moment at the warehouse, and they seem to suggest that not only does this establish responsibility under Article 7(3) as a superior, but also from that failure to intervene that you should infer his intent that those killings should take place. Your Honours, the evidence does suggest that there were two member of the 2nd Sekovici Detachment at the warehouse. According to hearsay evidence presented during the Prosecution case, one of them was named Krsto Dragicevic, and he asked to be relieved of his duties along the road where he was deployed, so that he could speak to the detainees about the fate of his father, who apparently had disappeared in the area sometime before. His commander, Rade Cuturic, perhaps concerned about what he might do, accompanied him. Now, Mr. Borovcanin, of course, does not know about this sequence of events. He is north on the road between Sandici and Konjevic Polje. The Prosecution theory of what happens next is that there is an execution, a planned execution at the Kravica warehouse, and that after this execution has started, the prisoners surge out, managed to grab a gun, kill Krsto, and injure Cuturic. Now, Mr. Borovcanin, when he does arrive back at the warehouse later on, is told something different. He is told that the prisoners, as I've mentioned earlier, had attempted to escape, and that no police were involved in the killings. The Prosecution presented no evidence showing which of these two accounts is correct. They presented no evidence about what happened to initiate the shooting. What we do know is that Mr. Borovcanin received frantic calls over his Motorola. He did not himself hear Cuturic's voice because he was out of range. All he heard was a response by someone at Sandici meadow. This is in Mr. Borovcanin's own statement, it's tentatively confirmed by Mr. Petrovic, and we will corroborate that evidence by presenting you with the results of field tests showing that a Motorola signal could not be heard between the Kravica warehouse and the position where Mr. Borovcanin was located. Now, by the time Mr. Borovcanin passes by the warehouse, Krsto is already dead, and Cuturic is on his way back to Bratunac with the injured hands. So, at least these two subordinates, or alleged subordinates, of Mr. Borovcanin, are not committing crimes at the warehouse. No evidence was presented during the Prosecution case showing that Mr. Borovcanin's other men were there at the warehouse, much less that he should have known that they were there. On the contrary, the evidence suggests that his units were not in control of the Kravica warehouse. They were spread out along the road further to the north preventing the column from crossing the road. You've also heard evidence that it was not the police who escorted the prisoners from the meadow, but that it was others; and you also have the testimony from one of the Muslim survivors at the warehouse, who said that the people at the warehouse guarding them were not the same as the ones guarding them at Sandici meadow. Your Honours, the Prosecution has also alleged, or perhaps just implied, that the warehouse was in an area controlled by Mr. Borovcanin's units, and for which he is therefore responsible. This is both factually and legally incorrect. Our experts will demonstrate that MUP units were not assigned distinct areas of responsibility in the military sense; rather, they were inserted into pre-existing areas of responsibility of the army units. The notion that the warehouse was within a MUP zone of responsibility is simply wrong. Second, you'll hear, also from our experts, that members of the Special Police, including Mr. Borovcanin, did not have ranks in 1995, in July 1995. He was not an officer, much less a superior officer. His sole authority was to command police officers in his units. He had no authority whatsoever to order any other soldier to do or not do anything. Then, Your Honours, leaving aside these deficiencies concerning who perpetrated the killings at Kravica warehouse, how it happened, and whether Mr. Borovcanin had any authority to intervene, we take issue with a more fundamental problem. The Prosecution argues that Mr. Borovcanin's failure to investigate further shows his intent. This is fundamentally contrary to basic principles of criminal law, not to mention human nature. Failing to make further inquiry to determine whether a crime has been committed cannot be equated with the intent to commit that crime. This is not a case where an accused sees his subordinates repeatedly commit crimes. This is a case of a single event bursting on the accused suddenly, where he has no basis to believe at the time that his men are involved, and, further, where he has no authority to intervene. Now, failing to intervene under those circumstances cannot lead to the inference that Mr. Borovcanin intended the commission of those crimes; and, in fact, you will hear evidence from two witnesses who will describe Mr. Borovcanin's reaction late on the afternoon of the 13th of July when he arrives back in Bratunac. Mr. Borovcanin arrived at the Bratunac police station in a very agitated state and asked to be connected to the Bratunac Brigade headquarters. His duty, as you'll hear from our experts, while subordinated to the VRS, was to report any criminal conduct to his military superiors. Even assuming, which we do not accept, that anyone from the 2nd Sekovici Detachment may have been involved at the Kravica warehouse unbeknownst to Mr. Borovcanin, his primary duty was to report what he knew about the commission or possible commission of crimes up his chain of command. As you will also hear from our experts, responsibility for further investigations and, if necessary, Prosecution, rested with the brigade authorities. That was prescribed by regulation but, more importantly, it's also reasonable and sensible in light of the transitory nature of Mr. Borovcanin's command. He doesn't have resources to undertake investigations, and he doesn't have jurisdiction over anyone other than his own men. In that context, it's more suitable that such reporting and such investigations occur to the brigade. Now, what about the alleged Krstic intercept? We will not be adducing any specific evidence on this. We contest that the person with whom General Krstic is speaking is Mr. Borovcanin. But even if it were Mr. Borovcanin, we think that when you view this rather anodyne conversation in light of the totality of the evidence, it hardly shows that Mr. Borovcanin was engaging in a broad criminal conspiracy to execute thousands of Muslim civilians or detainees. Your Honours, you are also going to hear or read evidence of the good character of Mr. Borovcanin. This is a man who has, and I quote, "a warrior's sense of honour"; a man who tries to find, and I quote again, "common sense compromises in times of crisis to avoid violence." Those are not my words, Your Honours; that's the opinion of an American general who worked with Mr. Borovcanin during the implementation of the Dayton Accords. In conclusion, Your Honours, our case is about adding context and perspective to the evidence that has already been presented by the Prosecution. We are confident that once you have the benefit of all that evidence, you will see that Mr. Borovcanin did not intend mass murder, that he did not intend forcible transfer, and that he did not intend any of the other crimes alleged against him. He was trying his best to deal with the humanitarian consequences of the takeover of territory on which there were 30.000 civilians who were terrified and desperate to leave. At the same time, he was trying to fulfill combat duties that had been assigned to him in response to a credible and real combat threat. This naturally involved taking prisoners. This is a normal, if perhaps unpleasant consequence of combat, and very serious crimes were subsequently committed against those detainees. But to lay that at the feet of Mr. Borovcanin, to say that he knew about that in advance without any meaningful evidence and by conflating his cooperation with others in the military affairs, the military offensive, is unjust and unfair. It verges, in fact, on an attempt to impose collective responsibility for those crimes without bothering with the essential elements of criminal responsibility such as individual intent. Your Honours, I'm relatively new to this case, and I wish to repeat that I'm honoured to be here before you and amongst respected colleagues, and I'm also deeply honoured to represent Mr. Borovcanin and to have had this opportunity to address you on his behalf. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Gosnell. Now, I think we can proceed with the first witness. Now, let me brief you a little bit on what is going to happen today. Due to unforeseen circumstances, we will need to stop at 13.25 instead of at 13.45, in order to try and gain a little bit from the time which would be lost. We have agreed to reduce the breaks from the usual time to 20 minutes. So we'll have two breaks as usual, but they will be of 20 minutes duration. The first one will be in about 12 minutes time. So, in the meantime, we can start with the first witness, and then we'll have a break at 10.20.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, to you, Professor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are most welcome to this Tribunal. As you know, you've been summoned as an expert witness by the Defence team for Ljubomir Borovcanin in this case. You will be starting your evidence, your testimony soon. Before you do so, our rules require that you enter a solemn declaration, the text which is being handed to you now, as to the effect that in the course of your testimony, you will be speaking the truth. Please go ahead, read it aloud, and that will be your solemn declaration with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. I solemnly declare that I will tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Please make yourself comfortable. Mr. Lazarevic, who will introduce himself to you shortly, will go first. He will then be followed by others on cross-examination. Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Dr. Bajagic. Of course, we had an opportunity to meet several times prior to this day; but for the record, I would ask you to -- I'm going to represent or introduce myself. My name is Lazarevic, and I'm part of the Defence team of Mr. Borovcanin. Now, for the record, please state your full name.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: My name is Mladen Bajagic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Just a little warning before we begin, since we both speak the same language, and in order to avoid a situation in which we might overlap, could you please be so kind to wait until I finish my question, and you can see that on the transcript in front of you. As soon as it stops, then you can start giving your answer; thereby, we shall avoid any possible problems. Dr. Bajagic, can you tell us the place and the date of your birth?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: I was born on the 5th April 1962 in Sarajevo, the then-Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina which was part of the SFRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Tell me where you finished primary and secondary schools?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: I finished my primary and secondary schools in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: After finishing secondary school, did you enroll in the university?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me which university, when did you graduate, what did you study?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: I enrolled in the faculty of political sciences at the Sarajevo university and graduated in 1988.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: After the university, did you acquire any other academic titles?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. In the period between 1997 and the year 2000, I attended masters degree studies at the faculty of political sciences at the Belgrade university; and, in the year 2000, I earned the title of master of political sciences.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: After that, I entered into the course for a Ph.D. and I defended my doctor's thesis in 2006, again at the faculty of political sciences in Belgrade; and, thereby, I earned the title of the doctor or the doctor's degree in the political science and international relations.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can you just tell me now, because I would like to go through shortly through your career, after the university, what was your first job?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Even before I graduated and during a period after I graduated and earned my bachelors degree, I worked in journalism, and I was also involved in the then-sociopolitical organizations that existed at the time in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: When you say "sociopolitical organizations," can you tell us a little bit more what that involves, because I suppose this is a rather foreign term to the people who are not from that region?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: At the time in all republics of the former Yugoslavia, there were a number of political organizations that work the under the umbrella of the then-League of Communists. Among them were the Alliance of the Socialist Youth and the Socialist Alliance of Working People.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can you tell us how your career progressed from that point onwards?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: In 1992, I found a job with the then-National Security Service, which was later to become the State Security Department of the Ministry of the Interior of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can you tell me, please, what kind of duties you discharged within the National Security Service of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Given that I had a university degree, I was given the job of an operational worker in the -- or the operative in the State Security Department.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: We'll take a break at 10.20 which is right now, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's have the break now, and as I said 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, next break will be at noon.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I'll bear this in mind. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Dr. Bajagic, before we took the break, you had told us that you found employment at the then-National Security Service of Republika Srpska and that you worked as an operative. Just to clarify things, what kind of duties does the post of an operative entail?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: This entails, to put it shortly, the realisation of intelligence and counter-intelligence activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Could you please explain in more detail, because we here are laymen, what you mean by the realisation of intelligence and counter-intelligence activities?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: That involved gathering intelligence information, preparation of intelligence studies, and passing them on to those who wielded political power. This was relative to all forms of endangerment of national security and the protection of national interests.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. While you were working at the then-National Security Service, which then later became the State Security Department, with respect to this first level on the ladder that you had, did you, for example, acquire any higher position in the hierarchy later on?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't. Throughout the whole period of my work at the State Security Department, I was an operative.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: How long did you work there?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: I worked for the State Security Department until the end of December 1995. When I left my job, I actually resigned at my own initiative.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: After that, what did you do? What kind of jobs did you do?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: From January 1996, I took permanent residence in Belgrade; and from September 1996, I started working at the then-police State Security Department as an assistant intern on the subject of the state security system.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: After that, did you advance through your teaching career?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. When I acquired my masters degree in political sciences, I was given an academic title of assistant. After that, I acquired the titles of lecturer, senior lecturer, and professor. At the police college, after I had acquired my Ph.D., I became a teacher -- or, actually, assistant professor at the State Security Department of criminology and police.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Are you still doing the same job?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am. I am working as a teacher at the State Security Department of criminology and police in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what subjects are you teaching?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: At the moment, I am teaching the following subjects: International security, the methodology of intelligence work, security systems, and terrorism and political violence. There are some other subjects, but they are of a more specialised nature and are taught at a masters level. I think what I just told you would suffice.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely. In addition to teaching, were you involved in scientific and research work as well?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Working at university invariably involves teaching and research work as well, so, yes, I was involved in research, both independently and as part of individual projects.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Have you published any scientific works? Of course, we are not going to go through all of them, but can you just highlight what of these papers would, in your view, be the most important ones?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: So far, I have published some 50-odd scientific articles in national and international magazines and proceedings, but I think the most important ones are monographies and textbooks that I have published so far.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us some of their titles, please?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about three monographies. The first one is entitled the "Role of the Intelligence Community in Foreign Policy, the Show Case of the US"; two publications of the monography entitled "World Security from Transparency to Secrecy," which deals with the structure and analyses of various intelligence systems existing in the world; and, finally, the fourth one is a textbook entitled "Basic Elements of Security."

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. During your professional career, were you a visiting professor at any other universities; and if you were, can you tell us which universities?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was. I worked at the faculty of political sciences in Belgrade, the faculty of security, and some privately owned universities in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Just a couple of questions about this, during your professional career, did you cooperate with any international organisations?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did, particularly within the framework of the project entitled "Reform of Police and Police Educational System in Serbia" with the OSCE and the Council of Europe.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And, just for the record, your expert report within the electronic system of this court is number 4D499, and your CV is 4D500. Let us now move to some other topic. Tell me, please, when was the first time you had contact with the Defence team of Mr. Borovcanin.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: That was in the spring of 2007. I think it was late April or early May, I'm not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: How was this contact established between you and Mr. Borovcanin 's Defence team?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: First, there were telephone contacts; then, we agreed to have some working meetings; and, then, we met in person.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us where this took place?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: In view of my professional commitment, I asked members of the Defence team to meet with me in my office at the Academy of Criminology and Police.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: What were you told at the time about the subject of your expert report?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Members of the Defence team of Mr. Borovcanin indicated that the subject of my expert report should be organisation and responsibilities of the Ministry of the Interior of Republika Srpska in the period 1992-1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And, of course, you accepted to act as an expert, and when your employment was formally acknowledged by the registry of this Tribunal, was that followed by any further contacts by the Defence team of Mr. Borovcanin?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were a number of telephone conversations and there were some meetings in person.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Did the Borovcanin Defence team provide you with the appropriate documentation necessary for drawing up your report?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. These meetings were precisely designed for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Apart from the document mentioned in your report, did Mr. Borovcanin give you some other documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] The transcript here says on page 30, line 23 -- no, it's 31, I am sorry: "... did Mr. Borovcanin give you some other documents." "The Defence of Mr. Borovcanin," this is what I meant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is there a need for me to repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: I understand the question, there is no need. No. The answer is no.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. As you were drafting your expert report, did you peruse any other documents not originally received from Mr. Borovcanin's Defence?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. I did use other documentation. I believed that the topic and the structure of the report that I chose to use required using some other references and research material available as part of the public sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Before coming to The Hague to testify on this occasion, did you ever visit The Hague before that?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, in late November, early December 2007. My stay here lasted for about six or seven days.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: What was the reason of your stay in The Hague in November 2007?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: As I have explained already, in my contacts with Mr. Borovcanin's Defence team, I expressed my desire to try and arrange such a visit on my part to The Hague and the Tribunal, in accordance with the procedure of course, the purpose of which was for me to see what it all looks like. I know now that it assisted me greatly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: During your stay in The Hague, did you have occasion to meet Mr. Borovcanin in person?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. Upon approval of those in charge at The Hague Tribunal, one afternoon during my stay was dedicated to a visit of mine to see Mr. Borovcanin at the Detention Unit in Scheveningen.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you alone with Mr. Borovcanin on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: No. There were three Defence team members in attendance as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Just one more thing, as best you can remember, how long did the meeting take?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: I think the meeting lasted for about an hour and a half or two hours with a short break. That was according to procedure, but I didn't may much heed to such details. In any case, at least an hour and a half.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: During are the meeting, what was your topic of discussion with Mr. Borovcanin and the Defence team members?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Primarily, we talked about the general methodological framework which would serve as a basis for drafting my expert report.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Be it Mr. Borovcanin or anyone else from his Defence team, did any of those people try to exert any influence on the conclusions of your expert report?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Given that the topic of my analysis and expert report was known to everyone, Mr. Borovcanin's Defence team members could only generally be familiar with certain individual elements of my expert report; however, they exerted no influence be it on the contents or the chapters of the report, and especially the conclusions. I would simply not have allowed that because finally I was the person signing the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You said already that during your stay in The Hague, you met with Mr. Borovcanin. Before that, that is to say, before November last year, had you known Mr. Borovcanin?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. Officially, we met in person in 2000. We were both participants of a scientific gathering dedicated to the topic of world terrorism. That gathering took place in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: The year is 2002.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Excuse me, for the record, what was the year?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. After the meeting in the Detention Unit in The Hague, did you ever meet with Mr. Borovcanin subsequently; and if so, in what circumstances?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, very briefly. I believe it was in early summer this year. I saw Mr. Borovcanin for a few minutes when he was visiting his family. I believe that was the occasion. It was a very brief encounter amounting to five or six minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me where that took place?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: We met in front of a house where Mr. Borovcanin's parents live, I believe. It is in the outskirts of Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Did anyone else attend this occasion?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, certain Defence team members did. Those people are also present in the courtroom today.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: How did it come about that you were in Bijeljina at the time?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: My sister lives in Bijeljina. I was visiting my family. Since I was in the area, I spoke on the phone with Defence team members, and I asked that I be allowed to undertake a short trip to Bijeljina, Srebrenica, and back. I was simply curious and I wanted to see that area. Although I hale from Bosanska Krajina, I never had visited those two towns before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: To close this topic, I wanted to ask you this: Between 2002, when you met Mr. Borovcanin for the first time, and coming to The Hague, did you meet with Mr. Borovcanin during that time?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Between what period?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Between 2002 and today?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correction for the transcript, page 34, line 11, the answer was "between 2002 and 2007," rather than "today."

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: To round off the topic, how would you describe your relationship with Mr. Borovcanin.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Well, since we only met on a couple of occasions, I can say that he is an acquaintance of sorts.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bajagic. Can you tell me what is before you on the desk?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Before me is a copy of my expert report as well as a binder with documents in chronological order that support my expert report; and I have some additional papers in my briefcase, but I can't place them on the table. There's no more room.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you explain briefly the structure of your report?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: As we know, the report is entitled "Minister of the Interior of the Republika Srpska, Organisation and Competence between 1992 and 1995." According to the contents, you can see that it consists of five chapters: Chapter 1, General Context; Chapter 2, Establishment and Development of the MUP of Republika Srpska; Chapter 3, Control and Command in the RS MUP; Chapter 4, Reporting and Informing in the MUP; finally, Chapter 5, Ranks and Functional Insignia in the RS MUP. Of course, preceding the chapters, there is a list of acronyms and abbreviations to refer to when reading the body of the text.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Another question: The five chapters, do they contain subchapters?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Certainly. There are five general topics discussed in the chapters; and in the first three chapters, there are subchapters.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to move on to the topic of your expert report.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is 4D499.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Under "General Context," you provided a definition of the police, at page 4 in the B/C/S and page 4 in the English in e-court. It is paragraph 4. There you state that the police can be defined as an organ of governmental authority, the purpose of which is to protect societal values ascribed to it through the law including any forceful means deemed necessary. If we start with this definition, what would be the basic function of the police?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Starting with this definition, as well as many other definitions of the police, generally speaking, it's basic function could be defined as serve and protect; that is to say, to implement tasks and duties in order to protect public law, security, and order, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: In your experience, the definition provided therein, does it only refer to the RS police, or is it universal in nature?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: This is certainly not something specific to the RS. It is a working definition used for the report and can be applied to any police organisation in the world.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your expert report, item 6, which is page 5 in the B/C/S and in the English version in e-court, save for the basic function of crime prevention and repression, you also mention the service segment. What did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: In contemporary police school of thought, it is said that the police is there is serve and protect. To protect means combatting crime, protecting law and order. As for the service or social service segment, that means that the police force should serve, which encompasses several duties and obligations within a society. If you wish, I can enumerate some of those: Assisting the elderly and infirm, assisting the young, assisting inebriated persons or persons who find themselves in similar states, as well as promoting safety and educating the society in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: If you now look at point 8, this is also on page 5 in both versions. Can you tell us what are, in your view, the basic groups of police tasks?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: In addition to this social service aspect of police work, another two major groups of police tasks are definitely maintaining law and order and fighting crime. Fighting crime, in general terms, involves both prevention and repression.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now move to another topic, and that would be security. Can you tell me, in general terms, what security involves? I would like to refer you to paragraph 11 in your report.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is on page 6 in B/C/S version and the same page in English.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 11 deals with national security, which necessitates full comprehension of the notion of national security. Security is a very wide notion difficult to be defined, but I will do my best to give you the brief version. Security has two aspects: An objective one and a subjective one. Objectively speaking, that implies absence of threat to an acquired values embraced by individuals or society, and also the absence of fear of loss of these acquired values. This is a very often used notion of security in defining this aspect scientifically. Security in every sense implies that this is one of the basic human needs, values, and interests; and, finally, security is most certainly one of the basic attributes and functions of a state.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Of course, this brings me to my next question. What is a security system?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Every state, in order to fulfill the functions that it's being established for, including security, must set up a certain system, as I call it here, the security system as a subsystem or part of the executive branch system. This implies forms of organising and functioning a society, or rather, a set of measures and activities pursued by organisations entrusted - I'm not going to quote precisely - with achieving and preserving security in the full sense of the word; and internationally, it has been recognised as state security.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at paragraph 14 on page 5, and page 7 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: What can you tell us about the subjects of the security system? How did you explain that in this particular paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: There is a multitude of various classifications of security subjects as basic elements of every security system. In my report, I just mentioned one of the possibilities in order to facilitate the further reading of my report. According to this classification that you can see here, the security system subjects can be divided into three groups. These are conventional, non-conventional, and supplementary subjects or elements of a security system.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you just tell us briefly something about these three systems? Can you tell us what conventional, non-conventional, and supplementary systems represent?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Conventional or, let's say, traditional or classic security systems definitely include Ministry of the Interior, i.e., the police; army as the second element; intelligence and counter-intelligence institutions and other institutions set up at the national level; judiciary; prosecutor's Office; customs; service inspections; and other organs entrusted with imposing criminal sanctions, et cetera. Non-conventional elements of security systems are legislature, depending on the nature of the political system, whether it has a parliament or an assembly; then there's executive organs; foreign affairs organs; and that would be it. Finally, bearing in mind one of the basic roles of the police, in addition to protects and serve, there are some additional elements that both the police, as well as other conventional and non-conventional organisations have, we can include local communities and local government; public services; educational institutions; scientific institutions; non-governmental organisations; religious institutions; and citizens, as individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. In this regard, what can you tell us about police as one of the security system elements?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Police represents in every sense, regardless of which state we are talking about, one of the pillars of security systems. To put it simply, there is not a modern state in the world that does not have its own police force.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your report, paragraph 18, page 8 in B/C/S, you use the term "administrative actions of police," and how are they classified?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: As I said, the purview and the competence of police are very precisely defined by various regulations and rules. Apart from the fact that these laws and bylaws, rules and regulations define the purview of the police, they also provide definitions of what legal authorisation and power police have in terms of in carrying out administrative actions within their scope of responsibilities. These are actually police duties or, as we define it in the part of the world where I come from, are police powers.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Can we now explain in more details the administrative activities of police?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: I am sorry. I did not give an answer --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting you.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: I did not give you an answer to the second part of your question. The science which deals with police says that administrative actions of police can be divided into two basic groups. These are administrative actions carried out by the police towards things and those applied to persons. Maybe later we will have an opportunity to speak about both.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you again, and I apologise for interrupting you. In July 1995, can you tell me which legal document or act governed the authority and the powers of the RS police?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: That was the Law on Internal Affairs passed in 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at Exhibit 4D358.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And in your folder, it's tab 67, in the binder.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: I apologise. Yes, I found it. I found the tab.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us first look at Article 40 of this law. It's on page 4 in B/C/S and page 8 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you see this Article 4 [as interpreted]?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me what police activity is stipulated by Article 4 [as interpreted]?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: As we can see, Article 40 defines the you powers of the police to issue --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us now move to Article 41. It's page 4 in B/C/S and pages 8 and 9 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me which administrative action is determined by Article 41?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: This involves checking ID papers in order to establish the identity of persons, and bringing these individuals before the organ in charge. So, actually, there's two powers inherent to this article: One is to check the ID, establish the identity; and then bring such a person to the organ in charge.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us now look at Article 42, the same page in B/C/S; and in English, it's page 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell what administrative action we are talking about here?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: This involves issuing information and warnings to individuals or summoning persons in order to give them notices and warnings?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's move now to Article 43, pages 4 and 5 in B/C/S, and pages 9 and 10 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: What administrative actions are we talking about here?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Article 43 speaks about bringing people into custody.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us move on now to Article 46, page 5 in B/C/S, pages 10 and 11 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: So, Article 46, what administrative action we are talking about here?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: This is one of the characteristic administrative actions that most police forces carry out, and that is the right to use vehicles and communication devices belonging to other people.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And in what way is this issue regulated?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Well, it reads here that in exception or circumstances, members of police and MUP can requisition or make use of private vehicles and communications devices, but provided that if they incur any costs in the process, they are obliged to refund the owner of the vehicle or the communications device.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's move on to Article 48, page 5 in B/C/S and page 11 in English.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to Article 48, the police is authorised to carry out administrative activities involving gathering of information and intelligence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now move on to Article 50, page 5 in B/C/S, and page 11 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me what administrative actions are envisaged by Article 50?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Article 50 envisages the following administrative activities by using oppression means. I can tell you more specifically that it involves the use of physical power, rubber trench, and service dogs, service mounted police force, water cannons, gas, and other means.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us look at Article 50 next --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: 51.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is pages 5 and 6 in the B/C/S; in the English version, it is page 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: What does this article prescribe in terms of use of firearms?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: It defines the police authority to use firearms. As far as I can see, it provides the conditions in which the police have the right to use this authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Article 52 is next. It's on the next page. In English, it is also page 12. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: What does Article 52 foresee?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Freely interpreted, I would say that it describes the procedure in which a firearm may be used in the sense that the firearm can only be used if all other means of force failed in implementing the police task. There's also an obligation of any authorised official entitled to carry and use a firearm to issue a warning prior to its use, and to, of course, keep in mind all other legal prerequisites that have to be met prior to using a firearm.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. During the proofing, you stated that this law was published in August 1995; but as far as we can see from the preamble, it was a revised text of the regulations passed before 1994, but were in force in July 1995 as well?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. It says, "amended and revised text in the preamble of the law on Internal Affairs"; however, the gist is the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I understand, in the English version, it says "amended and revised text." What we suggest as being the correct interpretation should be "consolidated."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. That can be taken care of in due course. Thank you for your observation, Mr. Lazarevic. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now that we went through some regulations defining the authority and powers of the RS MUP, can you compare that with the regulation of other countries pertaining to the same topic? Are there any similarities or differences?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Certainly. There are two different approaches two regulating the administrative activities of the police forces elsewhere in the world. Some define general authority and subsequently going into the details and specifics of those. There are examples which clearly and in a detailed fashion describe all of the different powers that such police forces have. Such police authority may not be defined only by the law on the police, but also as part of some other laws such as the laws in combatting organised crime, terrorism, et cetera. Some such examples are cited in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us go to item 33 of your expert report.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is on page 11 in the B/C/S; and in the English, it is page 12 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I came across a term there, "a state of national necessity." What do you refer to there?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: A state of national necessity is not specific to Republika Srpska alone. Any state can be in a state of peace or in a state of war or other circumstances. Such a state can be referred to a state of national necessity which may include several different situations.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: This term, "state of national necessity," how can it be applied to the situation in Republika Srpska between 1992 and 1996?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Certainly. The most extreme variations of a state of national necessity is a state of immediate threat of war and a state of war. Such two types of states of national necessity apply to the situation that was in place in Republika Srpska in that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please in e-court have a look at the next document, 4D219.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: In your binder, it is tab 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like us to have a look at page 2 in B/C/S and at page 4 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: It is the 35th amendment of the RS constitution published in the Official Gazette of the Republika Srpska on the 11th of November 1994 in Sarajevo. Please have a look at amendment 35. Pursuant to this amendment, what is the difference between a state of immediate threat of war and a state of war?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: The difference between an immediate threat of war and the state of war means that in the state of war, the fighting had already begun; whereas, a state of immediate threat of war entails the existence of a serious and invariable threat that armed conflict may ensue.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We also have a state of emergency in subitem (3). Can you tell us what that is according to the amendment?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: It means that there was a danger of safety, human rights, and freedoms, or normal functioning of constitutional organs, according to amendment 35.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Let us have a look at item 2 of amendment 35. Do the authorities of the president of Republika Srpska increase as opposed to certain other governmental organs, say the assembly, in such a state?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Since it is up to the assembly to decide on the issue of war and peace, in item 2, it say that is should the national assembly be unable to meet, the state of immediate threat of war is pronounced by the president. According to this amendment, he is authorised to declare the state of immediate threat of war and of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: So far, we have been discussing the constitutional amendments in 1994, when they were passed. The state of national necessity, as such, did it exist in Republika Srpska even prior to 1994?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: The state of national necessity existed in Republika Srpska prior to 1994 in the form of an immediate threat of war. I believe it was April 1992 when in the territory of the then-Serbian Republic of BiH, subsequently Republika Srpska, that the state of immediate threat of war was declared. I believe, according to the documentation I perused, that it was the 14th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us have a look at that document in e-court. It is 4D527.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: In your binder, it is tab 3. Is this the decision that you referred to?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it. It is a decision to declare an imminent threat of war and mobilisation throughout the territory of the republic. If my memory was correct, and it seems that is it was, it was the 15th of April 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The state of national necessity you referred to, does it have any impact on the police as regards its authorities and administrative activities it may undertake?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Certainly, it does. In any case, any state of national necessity impacts directly on the work and functioning of state bodies, including the police which in such situations, and according to some other legal regulations in relation to a declared threat of war, receive special tasks and also special administrative activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: What was the law that prescribe the functioning of the police in states of national necessity?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: It is the law and the application of the Law on Internal Affairs in times of an immediate threat of war, dated November 1994, to be precise the 29th of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. During your testimony, we will frequently refer to that law. For now, I only have a general question concerning that. The administrative activities foreseen by the law, were they of permanent nature?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
